The Black buffalo (Ictiobus niger) is a long-lived catostomid native to the Mississippi River basin. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] have documented maximum longevity of approximately 8,760 days [am = approximately 8,760 days] in this species, making it one of the most durable members of its genus. Growth trajectory analyses indicate that females attain their total length at puberty at 47 centimeters [Lp = 47 centimeters], a size typically reached after several years of sustained somatic expansion. The wet weight at puberty is estimated at 1.3 kilograms [Wwp = 1.3 kilograms] based on length-weight regressions developed from extensive field collections. This substantial mass at maturation likely reflects the considerable energetic investment required to achieve reproductive competence in a large-bodied riverine teleost.

Reproductive output in the Black buffalo has been the subject of focused investigation, particularly given its phylogenetic relationship to the bigmouth buffalo (Ictiobus cyprinellus). Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate has been calculated from observed fecundity and spawning frequency data. Specifically, females deposit approximately 750,322 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 750,322 eggs per spawning event], and they complete roughly one spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per year] under optimal thermal regimes. This annual reproductive investment places the Black buffalo among the more fecund iteroparous freshwater fishes in North America. The large clutch size is consistent with a life-history strategy that balances high fecundity against the substantial losses typical of pelagic egg and larval stages in riverine environments.

Neonatal body mass in the Black buffalo is remarkably small relative to adult dimensions, reflecting the species' reliance on high fecundity and external fertilisation. The wet weight at birth is just 0.0048 grams [Wwb = 0.0048 grams], a value derived from the average diameter of newly fertilised eggs, which measure approximately 2.1 mm in diameter. Upon eclosion, the prolarva emerges with a prominent yolk sac and commences a lecithotrophic phase that sustains development until the mouth-opening stage and the onset of first exogenous feeding. At a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], this initial period of yolk absorption proceeds at a predictable rate, and the tiny body mass at hatching underscores the species' highly altricial developmental mode. The contrast between the 0.0048 gram hatchling and the eventual adult size is striking.

Asymptotic body size in the Black buffalo represents the upper bound of somatic growth and is attained only after many years of continuous feeding. The ultimate total length reaches 123 centimeters [Li = 123 centimeters] in the largest individuals examined, a measurement documented from museum specimen series and long-term fishery-independent surveys across the species' range. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight is 28.7 kilograms [Wwi = 28.7 kilograms], placing the Black buffalo among the heaviest catostomids in North America. The relationship between length and mass is strongly allometric, with mature individuals exhibiting a deep, robust body form that contributes to their substantial mass. At the stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], maximum body size is achieved over a lifespan that commonly exceeds two decades, a growth strategy that prioritises prolonged somatic investment in a stable riverine habitat.

Comparative life-history analyses within the genus Ictiobus reveal that the Black buffalo occupies a distinct ecological niche characterised by slow maturation and high longevity. Under the consistent thermal conditions of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], females reach their total length at puberty of 47 centimeters [Lp = 47 centimeters] and corresponding wet weight at puberty of 1,300 grams [Wwp = 1,300 grams], after which they invest heavily in annual reproductive output. The maximum lifespan of 8,760 days [am = 8,760 days] observed at this temperature is similar to that reported for the closely related bigmouth buffalo, though the Black buffalo achieves a slightly greater ultimate total length of 123 centimeters [Li = 123 centimeters] at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Constrained by the energetic demands of a large body size and iteroparous reproduction, this species exemplifies a conservative life-history strategy common among long-lived freshwater teleosts inhabiting stable, productive large-river systems.
